Vairamuḍi
(‘crown of diamonds’)
------------------------------------------
The consecrated images of gods in Hindu temples—whether firmly secured inside the sanctum or used as उत्सव-mūrtis (processional images)—are treated with great respect. It is the strong belief of the devoted Hindus that god lives in them in a subtle form. Consequently even the utsavamūrtis, especially on important festival days, get the same worship and treatment as the original icon inside the shrine.
There can be no better example for this than the उत्सवमूर्ति of Celuva-nārāyaṇasvāmin in his temple at मेल्कोटे which is situated at a distance of 36 kms. (22 miles) from Mandya, the district headquarters, in the Karnataka State.
The brahmotsava—the biggest festival of the year—of this temple is generally held during March. The most important day during this period is the वैरमुडि उत्सव, the festival of the वैरमुडि. On this day the उत्सवमूर्ति is decorated with the वैरमुडि, the ancient crown of diamonds of unknown origin, and taken round the town in a procession.
According to the स्थलपुराण or the local legends it was originally the crown of Lord नारायण. Once the demon king विरोचन stole it and ran away. However, गरुड, the eagle-mount of the Lord, recovered it after defeating the demon. When he was returning, he saw कृष्ण and offered it to him, realising that he was the इन्चर्नतिओन् of नारायण himself. कृष्ण asked him to put it on the head of the image of Celuvanārāyaṇasvāmin at मेल्कोटे. Since it perfectly fitted the image, गरुड returned happily, leaving it there.
This crown is kept safely in the district treasury at Mandya. On the day of the festival, the casket containing it is brought, under heavy police protection, to मेल्कोटे, receiving worship on the way in several places. At the entrance of the town, the casket is transferred to a decorated palanquin and carried to the temple.
Since, as per tradition, it is not to be exposed to sunlight, it is worn on the head of the उत्सवमूर्ति by the chief priest at night, around 9 p.m. Then the image is taken round the main streets in a procession by placing it on a वाहन (vehicle) shaped like the kṣīrābdhi or the milky ocean. It returns to the temple before sunrise (around 4 a.m.). The Vaira-muḍi is then transferred to the casket and sent back to the treasury.
This festival is the most spectacular of all and is witnessed by lakhs of devotees.

vairāgya
------------------------------------------
Vairāgya or absence of attachment or renunciation is the second of the four sādhanas listed under ‘sādhanacatuṣṭaya’. It is a natural consequence of विवेक or discrimination. It pertains to all objects of pleasure, whether of this world or of the next.
The highest state of वैराग्य is that in which the मिन्द् is absolutely undisturbed even though an object of temptation is near at hand and can easily be enjoyed (vide Yogasūtras 1.15).

vairāgīs
------------------------------------------
Vairāgīs or bairāgīs are religious अस्चेतिच्स् of any of the Vaiṣṇava orders. They wear white clothes and apply ūrdhva-पुण्ड्र (vertical religious mark) on their foreheads, made of white clay and red pigment. They generally wear their hair as a crown and may also grow beard.
There are several sects and subsects among them.
